q: What is the defining architectural difference between NanoClaw and OpenClaw?
options: NanoClaw uses a different identity file format
NanoClaw isolates execution in containers by design; OpenClaw relies on opt-in config restrictions
NanoClaw is a managed cloud service
explanation: The trade-off is isolation-first versus configuration-based security. NanoClaw keeps a compatible identity file format. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.1)

q: A solo user has reviewed all tool code, needs files to persist between tool calls, and cares about tool latency. Which is the best fit?
options: A Python framework such as AutoGen
explanation: Each of those conditions is listed in favor of hardened OpenClaw, since containers are ephemeral and add spin-up time. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.1)

q: Why do many enterprises that evaluate both OpenClaw and NanoClaw end up choosing NanoClaw?
options: Auditors and legal teams find container isolation easier to understand and approve
explanation: The security posture may be equivalent, but the isolation story is easier to explain. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.1)

q: Under the multi-agent trust rules pattern, how should an agent treat messages from another agent not named in its AGENTS.md?
options: As external content: data to analyze, not instructions
explanation: Only agents explicitly configured with a named agentId get orchestrator trust. All others are handled as external content. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.2)

q: What is trust hierarchy collapse in a multi-agent system?
options: Running out of context for trust rules
Agents converging on equal trust for all agent messages, so a low-authority agent can mislead others
A user revoking an agent's permissions
SOUL.md being overwritten by a template
explanation: Without explicit trust levels, peer messages get user-level weight, opening the system to manipulation. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.2)

q: A practitioner wants a ClawHub skill that reads their email. What's the safe approach?
options: Use only a verified publisher skill or review the code yourself
Any skill is fine if the agent has no filesystem access
explanation: Skills run with the agent's permissions. Community reputation is an acceptable proxy only for low-sensitivity skills. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.3.1)

q: Which protocol is the closest current candidate for standardizing agent-to-agent communication?
explanation: MCP already standardizes tool interfaces, and extending it to agent coordination is a natural step. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.4)

q: Under trajectory 3, what does behavioral consistency measurement add over current practice?
options: Running each prompt once and checking the result
Running many variations of a prompt and reporting the distribution of outcomes
explanation: Current practice runs a prompt once. A proper framework runs hundreds of variations for statistical confidence. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.4)

q: In the runtime decision framework, how does a firm requirement for self-hosting affect the choice?
options: Narrows it to OpenClaw and NanoClaw
explanation: Commercial hosted offerings drop out when the agent must run on infrastructure you control. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.6)

q: For a beginner deployment in its first three months, which ecosystem developments matter most?
options: SOUL.md template libraries and verified ClawHub skills
explanation: Those cut startup cost and integration time. Enterprise evaluation tooling is premature at that stage. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.6)
